Proposal title: Amadeus Cloud Platform on Google Cloud: Architecture, Trade-offs, and Multi-Cloud Direction
Description:
After five years of building and operating our cloud platform on Azure, a shopping business case has prompted us to design and begin delivering an Amadeus Cloud Platform on Google Cloud Platform (GCP). This session shares where we are today: the current platform architecture on GCP, the decisions behind it, and what it means for teams used to Azure-first patterns.

We’ll walk through the platform’s foundational design (organization/landing zone structure, networking, identity and access, security guardrails, deployment patterns, and observability) and highlight the most important differences compared to Azure—both in cloud concepts and in day-to-day implementation. We’ll also summarize the pros and cons identified so far, including operational considerations, scalability and reliability trade-offs, and cost/effort implications as we build towards production readiness.

To close, we’ll briefly outline our multi-cloud strategy: why we’re investing in GCP alongside Azure, how we’re balancing cloud-native capabilities with portability, and what the next milestones look like for the platform.

Proposal title: Making LLMs Behave Smarter in Development
Description:
Have you ever wondered why a model, trained on the entire knowledge of internet, sometimes still hallucinates about a library that doesn't exist, keeps forgetting small details as time goes by, or gets your current existing code (or your prompt itself) completely wrong?

We often think of LLMs as some real person standing right in front of us and chatting with us, but underneath, what drives its "next-token prediction" mechanism is actually the application of heavy linear algebra with backpropagation, together with probability theory. Understanding this architecture and realizing its powerful sides (as well as its flaws) is the first step towards making effective use of these tools.

In this 25-minute talk, we will focus on __**context window management**__. 

We are going to explore why "chatting" with LLMs is the wrong paradigm for engineering tasks, why outdated information persists even in top-tier models (and features like web search or RAG cannot fully overcome it), and how can we -at least partially- take manual steps in solving the current problems of LLM usage in development. 

# Content
We are going to go over some simple but verified, researched "tips and tricks" for the purpose of reaching reliability while using LLMs: 
#### "Frontloading"
What I like to describe as "Frontloading" (a technique to exploit attention mechanisms of LLMs by placing critical keywords and sentences with upmost importance at the very beginning and end of your prompts)
#### The "One-shot" approach
Why you should be starting a new chat for every major task and performing manual conversation summarization, rather than letting the agent (or the text editor/IDE itself) dissect and dilute the context of your past conversation history
#### GitIngest
A new, simple, small, but very powerful web-based tool that allows you to dump specific GitHub path URLs (like documentation folders of frameworks, tools, or libraries) into a single Markdown file
#### Custom Context Injection
How to make use of custom Markdown (.md) files together with GitHub Copilot custom instructions in a meaningful way.
#### A brief look at other new cutting-edge tools currently under development
Finally, we'll only have a brief look at the cutting-edge, still-under-development tools like __**specs.md**__ and __**btca**__ to automatize what we discussed earlier. 
##### **specs.md**
Thanks to specs.md,  instead of asking an AI to "build a login page", you can first collaborate with the AI to write a detailed specification in a Markdown file. Once the spec is finalized, you "freeze" it, and the AI agent uses it as its main guide for generating code. It is aimed at preventing hallucinations by forcing the model to follow a documented plan rather than making probabilistic guesses. 
##### **RAG-as-a-Service (?): btca (better context for agents)**
btca (btca.dev) is a tool and protocol currently under development, to solve the "outdated knowledge" problem in LLMs and 'streamline' the process of providing it with up-to-date context. 
You add a btca.config to your project; then, it finds your dependencies by scanning your repository for files related to dependency management (requirements.txt, package.json, pom.xmls etc...) and fetches the latest documentation, for agents to use. It's being designed to automatically inject the most recent API references into your agent's context window.

Proposal title: "Threat Modeling as Code: How Structure Enables AI Assistance"
Description:
**Threat Modeling as Code: How Structure Enables AI Assistance**

As architectures grow more complex, threat modeling must scale with our systems. This session explores how structured threat models unlock multiple perspectives, reusability, and AI collaboration—while shifting focus from layout to security logic.

- **Modeling over layout** How YAML specifications automatically generate Threat Dragon diagrams—letting you focus on security design (actors, flows, boundaries, threats) instead of manually arranging boxes and lines

- **Multiple views from one source** Use tags to generate different stakeholder perspectives (full architecture, high security flows, subsystem views) without duplicating models

- **Reusability through composition** Extract and recombine threat model components across projects—define once, reuse everywhere

- **Enabling AI assistance** How structured data enables AI to help with model creation, gap analysis or threat suggestion

**Key insight**
When you model security as structured data, you focus on what matters—trust boundaries, data flows, threat scenarios—not diagram aesthetics. Multi-perspective views, component reuse, and AI readiness follow naturally.

For everyone involved in security by design—security specialists, architects, developers, and engineering teams.

Participants will walk through the entire lifecycle of an AI agent, from deploying the Llama Stack on Red Hat OpenShift AI to integrating advanced capabilities like Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Model Context Protocol (MCP), and multi-framework agent orchestration.

This hands-on workshop on building agentic AI applications using Llama Stack, LangGraph, Langfuse, FastAPI and FastMCP on Red Hat OpenShift AI. This lab series takes you from deploying your first Llama Stack instance to building AI agents that interact with enterprise systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

What You Will Learn
Architecting Agentic Systems: Understand the Llama Stack ecosystem and how it standardizes interactions between LLMs, tools, and memory.

Hands-on Deployment: Deploy Llama Stack on a production-grade Kubernetes environment (Red Hat OpenShift).

Tool Use & Connectivity: Integrate "Search" tools and utilise the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external data sources.

Agent Orchestration: Compare and build agents using different approaches, including native Llama Stack Agents, LangGraph for complex state management, and Langflow for visual low-code design.

Proposal title: Crypto 101: How Certificates Keep the Internet running
Description:
In today’s rapidly evolving digital environment, cryptography and certificates form the foundation of how organizations establish trust, protect data, and secure communications. As businesses shift toward cloud, automation, and zero trust models, understanding how these mechanisms work is no longer optional — it’s essential for ensuring resilience and preventing avoidable outages. This session provides a simplified, high level look at how cryptography enables confidentiality and integrity, and how digital certificates validate identity and secure interactions across our platforms. We will also explore the certificate lifecycle, why effective management is critical, and how shortening public certificate validity timelines are reshaping operational expectations. The goal is to help the audience clearly understand the hidden infrastructure behind trust — and the risks and opportunities associated with it.
 
Key Topics:
•	Basics of Cryptography — How encryption, hashing, and keys build the foundation of digital security
•	Symmetric & Asymmetric Encryption — Why modern systems use a hybrid approach
•	TLS Handshake — How secure communication channels are negotiated
•	Digital Certificates & Their Purpose — Identity, trust, and secure communication
•	Certificate Lifecycle Management — Issue, deploy, renew, revoke
•	Chain of Trust — Root, intermediate, and server certificates
•	Public Certificate Timelines — Impact of shorter validity periods on operations
•	Associated Complexities — Operational risks, outage prevention, and compliance requirements

real-time ingestion of streaming data from operational systems,
detection of business situations using rules and conditions (thresholds, patterns, correlations),

We will show how Azure Fabric simplifies real-time detection by combining event ingestion, analytics, and rule-based activation in a unified, SaaS platform—allowing teams to move from reactive monitoring to proactive detection, while maintaining scalability, governance, and operational simplicity.

Proposal title: From Cloud to Basement - my personal journey to self hosting everything*
Description:
TL;DR: A personal, practical look at why I ditched using proprietary software on the cloud and instead rebuilt my digital life using only open source running on hardware at home.
-----
While Amadeus has spent the past years moving from self‑hosted systems in Erding to Microsoft Azure, I’ve been heading in the opposite direction—away from cloud services and proprietary platforms, and toward running (mostly) open‑source software on hardware in my own basement.

Why make that shift? Recent events have shown how fragile our dependence on centralized services can be: the OVH data‑center fire in Strasbourg, major DNS outages at Cloudflare, and even governments blocking access to parts of the internet. Add to that the growing pressure on cloud and software providers to introduce backdoors, and the result is a landscape where user data, privacy, and autonomy feel increasingly at risk. At the same time, subscription costs keep climbing. It’s no surprise that more people are looking for digital sovereignty—control over their data, their infrastructure, and their costs.

In this session, I’ll walk through my own journey back to self‑hosting, using real examples from my setup, including:

- Network and infrastructure
- Hypervisor, storage, and backup
- Remote access
- Self‑hosted applications  
  - Docker, reverse proxying, note taking, flight & country tracking, file storage, photo backup, LLMs for chat and coding, and plenty more
- Future evolution of the setup

My goal is to show that self‑hosting isn’t just for people with racks of hardware and endless free time. You can build something powerful—or something simple—whether you have a dedicated server room or just an old laptop or Raspberry Pi. If this talk nudges you to start your own journey, or simply demystifies what’s possible, then it has done its job.

Disclaimer: This is one person’s setup, shaped by personal needs and preferences. It’s not perfect, and it’s certainly not the only way to do things.

Proposal title: From bad architecture to a (maybe) better architecture
Description:
## 1. How the PoC Became a Production Problem
I started this project by building a simple Proof of Concept meant only to validate the integration between a traditional operational workflow and an AI component. My intention was always to discard the PoC afterward and build a proper, production‑ready cloud‑native architecture. But inside the organization, that distinction wasn’t fully understood. People began using the PoC as if it were a real system, even loading production data into it. Suddenly I found myself explaining why something that “already worked” couldn’t support real workloads, why it lacked security, resilience, observability, and why keeping it in production was far more expensive and risky than rebuilding it correctly. What seemed like a technical issue quickly turned into a deeper cultural and economic challenge: the team didn’t understand the purpose—or the limitations—of a PoC.

## 2. What I Did to Fix It
To move forward, I focused on educating the team and communicating clearly what was at stake. I walked them through the risks, the missing engineering practices, and the long‑term costs of relying on a prototype. Then I led the migration toward a robust cloud‑native architecture with proper security, CI/CD, observability, data governance, and scalable integration with AI. We ran both systems in parallel, migrated data safely, and gradually decommissioned the PoC without impacting operations. In the end, I not only delivered a stable, secure, and scalable platform, but also helped shift the organization’s understanding of what it means to build technology the right way—showing that overcoming cultural resistance can be just as important as solving the technical problems.

And that is precisely the purpose of this talk: to walk you through both sides of the journey. I want to show the architecture not only from a technical perspective—how it was designed, secured, scaled, and migrated—but also from the cultural perspective, where the biggest challenges often live. My goal is to illustrate how technical excellence and cultural alignment must work together, and how understanding both is essential when transforming a PoC into a real, reliable, cloud‑native solution.

Proposal title: Why Your Azure Disk Isn’t Slow — Your VM Is: Understanding and Fixing Throughput Bottlenecks
Description:
Cloud workloads can run surprisingly slow even when backed by high‑end Premium or Ultra disks. The real culprit is often overlooked: Azure Virtual Machines have their own IOPS and throughput caps, and these limits can silently throttle disks that are otherwise capable of much higher performance. This mismatch leads to warnings such as “The current VM size supports 23 MBps while attached disks require 160 MBps.”

In this fast, practical, engineering‑focused session, we’ll break down how Azure’s storage pipeline works—uncached I/O paths, cached I/O behavior, baseline vs burst throughput, and the performance limits defined by different VM and disk SKUs. You’ll learn why attaching a higher‑tier disk does not automatically guarantee higher performance, and how to read Azure’s published SKU specifications to identify mismatches before they become production bottlenecks.

The session includes a lightweight, Azure‑Monitor‑free demonstration using standard benchmarking tools such as fio or DiskSpd to validate real disk throughput and clearly illustrate VM‑level bottlenecking. We’ll also walk through a simple, repeatable framework for selecting the right VM size based on workload throughput needs, disk requirements, and expected traffic bursts.

Attendees will leave with the knowledge and tools needed to prevent disk throttling, size their infrastructure more effectively, and ensure their workloads achieve the performance they were designed for—without guesswork, surprises, or expensive over‑provisioning.

Proposal title: From Reactive to Proactive: Self‑Healing for Operational Excellence
Description:
As Amadeus accelerates its cloud migration, operational stability increasingly depends on fast, reliable responses to frequent but repetitive infrastructure and application issues. Traditionally, many of these incidents require manual intervention—leading to delayed recovery, operational fatigue, and increased risk of customer impact.
This talk introduces the Self‑Healing Engine (SHE), a proactive automation approach that detects, diagnoses, and remediates operational issues in real time—without human intervention where it is safe to do so. By integrating monitoring, alerting, orchestration, and ITSM workflows, SHE moves operations from a reactive firefighting model to an intelligent, automated recovery model.
The session will cover:
1) The problem statement behind self‑healing in large‑scale cloud platforms
2) The architecture and process flow of the Self‑Healing Engine
3) Real production use cases implemented with Deployment Manager and Argo CD
4) Measurable impact, including significant reduction in manual effort and MTTR
5) How to balance autonomy with control using guardrails and human‑in‑the‑loop mechanisms

Attendees will gain practical insights into designing, governing, and scaling self‑healing systems in complex cloud environments.

What Attendees Will Learn

How to identify operational issues suitable for self‑healing
A reference architecture for building a self‑healing platform
How monitoring, alerting, orchestration, and ITSM integrate end‑to‑end
Lessons learned from real infra and functional self‑healing implementations
Best practices to avoid risks like false positives and over‑automation

Platform Engineers
DevOps & SRE teams
Cloud Engineers
Engineering Leads and Architects
Anyone interested in improving operational reliability through automation

Proposal title: Small Steps, Big Impact: How Tiny Actions Transformed Our Team
Description: Every transformation starts with a story—and ours began with a backlog that felt overwhelming and costs that kept creeping up. Instead of sweeping changes, we focused on tiny, intentional actions: changing the way we work, improving communication, celebrating wins, and aligning priorities. Over six months, these small steps led to a 48% reduction in backlog, cost per PI closed reduced by 25%, efficiency increased by 40%, and—most importantly—a team that felt heard, valued, and motivated. In this talk, I’ll share the journey behind these results, the leadership habits that made the difference, and how you can spark your own ripple effect of success—one small action at a time.

Proposal title: Kafka: The Art of Building Systems That Never Wait
Description: Waiting is the enemy of scale. Kafka redefined how distributed systems communicate by embracing asynchrony, durability, and replayable history. We’ll unpack the beauty of Kafka’s design, compare it with traditional messaging systems, explore real-world implementation patterns, and learn what happens when Kafka itself breaks—and why that’s part of its brilliance.

Proposal title: Inside the Mind of a Machine: Demystifying Large Language Models
Description:
Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT appear magical from the outside—but beneath the surface lies a clear, understandable system that anyone can learn. This talk takes the audience on a guided tour through the full lifecycle of an LLM: from massive internet‑scale pretraining datasets, to the mathematics of tokens and transformers, to the post‑training processes that shape their behavior, reasoning, and personality.
We’ll explore how these models “think,” why they hallucinate, how they use tools, and why their intelligence can feel uneven or “jagged.” Along the way, we’ll build simple mental models for understanding their psychology—how they learn, how they store knowledge, how they infer context, and why they sometimes struggle with something as simple as spelling.
Designed for a general audience, this talk connects the technical foundations—tokenization, attention, neural network internals, supervised fine‑tuning, reinforcement learning, and RLHF—to the practical reality of working with AI today. The goal is to replace mystery with intuition, and empower everyone to use these systems more effectively, creatively, and responsibly in their work and life.
By the end, the audience will not only understand how these AI systems are built, but also how to think with them, think about them, and anticipate what’s coming next in the rapidly evolving world of machine intelligence.

Proposal title: Hey, Quarkus on JVM, can you get any faster? Towards faster builds and faster startup of Quarkus apps on JVM.

Speaker: Guillaume Smet (Red Hat /IBM)

Quarkus is faster than your traditional Java framework, we all know that, right? But can it get faster than itself?

We've spent years obsessing over Quarkus startup time and runtime performance. Build times, on the other hand, didn’t get nearly the same attention. And that was a mistake. Faster builds mean a tighter feedback loop for developers and fewer resources burned in CI.

In this session, we'll start with an overview of the work we've done in recent releases to significantly speed up the build of Quarkus JVM applications.

Now that we got our builds faster, could we also start our JVM applications faster?
As it turns out, yes. We'll present what Project Leyden and AOT class loading can bring to Quarkus (and, more broadly, to Java itself). We’ll cover the improvements we've made, the limitations we're still wrestling with, and why Leyden is reshaping the Java startup performance landscape.

Proposal title: From Logs to Root Cause: Building True Observability
Description:
In today’s complex distributed systems, traditional monitoring is no longer enough. Dashboards and alerts can tell you that something is wrong, but they rarely explain why it’s happening. This talk explores the art and science of true observability—the ability to understand your system’s behavior in production, detect unknown failures, and quickly identify root causes.

We will dive into the five pillars of observability—metrics, logs, traces, events, and context—and uncover common pitfalls that make telemetry ineffective. Using real-world examples and architectural patterns, you’ll learn how to design systems that are self-explanatory, scalable, and resilient.

Attendees will gain practical insights into:

How to correlate logs, metrics, and traces for end-to-end visibility

Best practices for instrumentation with OpenTelemetry

Designing observability architectures that support SLO-driven reliability

Avoiding hidden traps like high-cardinality metrics, broken trace propagation, and telemetry bottlenecks

By the end of this session, you’ll understand how to move beyond reactive monitoring to proactive root-cause analysis, ensuring your systems are both observable and reliable.

Proposal title: Agentic AI, RAG, and MCP: Architecting on MongoDB's Single Data Layer
Description:

The industry’s default response has been to bolt together a fragmented mess of vector stores, state databases, and custom APIs.

Proposal title: Architecture as Code
Description:
Corporations spend millions of dollars and thousands of hours onboarding new people to development teams and troubleshooting incidents where nobody knows who owns what. Tribal knowledge remains locked in individuals' heads while PowerPoint diagrams and Visio files scatter across shared drives like "a novel written on napkins and sticky notes." Traditional tools simply cannot handle modern enterprise complexity.

This workshop introduces Architecture as Code (AaC), a paradigm shift that treats architectural artifacts as version-controlled software assets. According to TOGAF, architecture encompasses the fundamental concepts and relationships of a system. "As Code" means expressing these in text-based, human-readable formats stored alongside the software they describe, with semantic URIs for cross-referencing and the ability to build holistic models from multiple sources.

Participants will learn to implement diagrams using tools like Structurizr DSL and Drawio, enforce policies with Open Policy Agent, and manage Architecture Decision Records programmatically. We will explore dimensions of expansion including metamodels, federated architecture models, progressive elaboration, and integration with AI agents for human-in-the-loop workflows. By the end of this session, participants will be equipped to establish a single source of truth that can be branched, merged, reviewed, and evolved - readable by both humans and machines.

Key Topics

Evolution from manual documentation to codified architecture

TOGAF definition and "As Code" principles

Infrastructure as Code, Diagrams as Code, Policy as Code

Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)

C4 Model and metamodel extension

Automated validation and compliance checking

Dimensions of expansion: progressive elaboration, integrations, federation

AI agents and human-in-the-loop architectural workflows

Proposal title: HRS and PDL Batch Job Stabilization
Description:
Problem Statement:
Between 2023 and 2025, the HRS and PDL systems have experienced recurring batch job failures due to a range of technical issues, including FO node capacity constraints, instability in the Object Store, and other system-level challenges. These failures have triggered repeated customer escalations, resulting in multiple IRS incidents.

Furthermore, the resource-intensive nature of recovery efforts has led to delays in data restoration—directly impacting customer-facing services and operational continuity.

Solution:
On PDL side, the History batch jobs are monolithic in nature, processing HRS data sequentially, peak by peak. This results in longer execution times, and any failure in a single HRS peak prevents data from successfully completed HRS jobs from being processed. To address this, we propose decomposing the monolithic PDL job into smaller, modular jobs—each corresponding to an individual HRS peak. This approach will enable parallel processing of HRS peak data within PDL, improving efficiency and fault tolerance.​

On HRS side, we already have data getting processed in parallel but we need to move jobs to batch pods to gain stability and benefit from the resources of an allocated Machine Set.​

Additionally, observability will be embedded into the solution by pushing batch job metrics (such as job duration, success/failure counts, and throughput) to Splunk. These metrics will be used to build dashboards and configure alerts, enabling real-time monitoring, faster issue detection, and improved operational transparency across the batch processing pipeline

Proposal title: SKube Design Patterns: Streamlining Microservice Development and Operations
Description:

In this talk we’ll see how SKube solves these challenges via patterns implemented across both Java and .NET cloud-native stacks:

* __Source2Chart__: auto-detect build-time capabilities and eliminate the need for Helm templates or Dockerfiles
* __Configuration source merging__: unify build-time and GitOps overrides into a single coherent runtime state
* __Multi-tenancy via dependency injection__: abstract tenant management from business code
* __OpenTelemetry instrumentation__: shift troubleshooting from log-first to trace-first, for faster root cause analysis

Proposal title: Turning DevOps Events into Engineering Insights : AI-Powered MCP for Change Management
Description:
Change management signals are fragmented across code repositories, CI/CD pipelines, and automation systems, making it difficult for engineers to understand the true impact of changes.

This talk presents a running AI-powered MCP (Model Context Protocol) system designed to analyze change management data by continuously ingesting DevOps events from tools such as Bitbucket, Jenkins, and AWX.

Using an event-driven architecture, the system builds evolving operational context as changes progress, allowing AI to surface recurring patterns, hidden dependencies, and meaningful engineering insights. Rather than automating actions, the focus is on supporting better human decision-making.

The session walks through the system architecture, how MCP grounds AI responses in real operational data, and the guardrails required to avoid hallucinations and false confidence. It also highlights what worked in practice, what didn’t, and how engineers interacted with AI-generated insights during real change scenarios.

Proposal title: Let's break things with Chaos Engineering
Description:
In today's complex and distributed systems, it is crucial to ensure their resilience and reliability.
Chaos Engineering is a discipline that helps engineers proactively identify weaknesses and vulnerabilities in their systems by intentionally injecting failures and disruptions (which mean finding issues by breaking things).

This workshop aims to provide you with a better understanding of Chaos Engineering and how it can be implemented in using the tool LitmusChaos.

Let's take on the role of Chaos scientists, creating disruptions through Chaos Experiments to simulate some network failures for example.
Breaking things is fun but let's discover how we can transform these disruptions into tests that validate the strength of systems using the notion of probes.
LitmusChaos also offers convenient features, such as code sharing, that we will explore together.

Description:
Accessibility isn’t just about improving user experience — it’s also a legal obligation. With regulations like the reinforced European Accessibility Act, teams working on digital products and content need to ensure their work meets the WCAG 2.x standards.
 
This two-hour workshop is a practical introduction to accessibility testing. You’ll learn how to spot common issues in both web interfaces and PDF documents, and how to test them using widely available tools.

What WCAG 2.x means in practice
Where accessibility issues often show up in websites and PDFs

Proposal title: Own Your Knowledge: The Obsidian Approach to Notes, Plugins, and the AI Era
Description:
Most note‑taking apps feel convenient: until they disappear, get decommissioned, remove features, or lock your data behind yet another subscription. **[Obsidian](https://obsidian.md/)** takes a completely different approach: every note is a simple Markdown file stored locally. You own the files, you control where they live, and nothing breaks if the app or a service shuts down.

In this talk, I’ll explain why Obsidian has become my core productivity/note taking tool for both work and personal life: not just because it's flexible, but because it enables things most note apps simply don't. Want a custom note structure? Write it. Need automation? Use Shortcuts/ scripts on your machine. Missing a feature? Install or develop a plugin. there are thousands, and the ecosystem keeps growing.

I’ll share how I use templates, the Tasks plugin, and daily/weekly notes to structure my work. Finally, we’ll explore how Obsidian’s Markdown‑based knowledge base integrates naturally with modern AI tools, turning your notes into a powerful private knowledge source you can query from your IDE.

Attendees will leave with a clear understanding of **why** Obsidian stands out, and **what it enables that other tools simply can’t**.

*(This talk is not related to Amadeus tools or internal systems. and it is NOT a sponsored talk! I genuinely love this tool :D)*

Description:
In this two‑hour hands‑on workshop, you’ll learn how to build a complete application using Spec‑Driven Development powered by GitHub Copilot, custom skills, structured instructions, and agent-based workflows. Instead of relying on traditional coding from scratch, you’ll define the system through clear specifications—and let Copilot generate consistent models, API routes, UI components, and logic.

Proposal title: Introducing AI driven development lifecycle (AI-DLC)
Description:
Speaker: Alexis Daguès - Principal Solutions Architect  (Amazon Web Services)

The AI-Driven Development Life Cycle (AI-DLC) represents a transformative approach to software engineering that positions AI as a central collaborator throughout the development process. Unlike traditional AI-assisted development methods, AI-DLC reimagines the entire software lifecycle through two key dimensions: AI-powered execution with human oversight and dynamic team collaboration. The methodology operates in three phases - Inception, Construction, and Operations - where AI initiates workflows while maintaining persistent context across all stages. This innovative approach delivers significant benefits including increased velocity, enhanced quality, improved market responsiveness, and better developer experience, all while ensuring critical human oversight and collaboration.

Proposal title: AI-Native development using MCP and Github Copilot
Description:
**Workshop Overview**

AI is rapidly becoming a core component of modern engineering workflows. However, many teams still see AI tools as productivity add-ons rather than foundational building blocks for system design.

This workshop is designed to bridge that gap.

Our goal is to make AI-native development concepts practical and accessible — even for engineers who have not yet worked directly with AI system components. By the end of the session, participants will understand the foundational ideas, see concrete examples, and gain hands-on experience building a simple MCP server.

On the practical side, we will focus specifically on developing an MCP server in detail, using two different examples to illustrate key patterns and design decisions. The emphasis will be on understanding how MCP works and how to experiment with it effectively.

We will combine conceptual clarity with guided implementation so that attendees leave with a solid understanding of MCP and the confidence to continue exploring and experimenting on their own.


**What Participants Will Learn**

1. Introduction to AI & LLMs (5 minutes)
A concise refresher on AI systems and large language models to align terminology and establish a common foundation.

2. General and Advanced Prompting Techniques (10 minutes)
Practical prompting strategies that move beyond basic instructions — including structured prompting, context control, and iterative refinement techniques.

3. Designing AI-Native Workflows (30 minutes)
How to shift from “using AI tools” to architecting workflows where AI is a first-class component, and your assistant in day-to-day life.
We will cover:
- AI-assisted development patterns
- Human-in-the-loop design
- Iterative experimentation cycles
- Practical workflow integration in engineering environments

4. What is Model Context Protocol (MCP)? (30 minutes)
An introduction to MCP and its role in enabling structured, scalable AI integrations.
Participants will understand:
- The motivation behind MCP
- How it manages context and tool interaction
- Why it matters for production-ready AI systems

5. Hands-On Session: Building a Simple MCP Workflow with GitHub Copilot (45 minutes)
A guided practical session where participants:
- Set up a simple MCP-based workflow
- Use GitHub Copilot to interact with it
- Experiment with modifications and extensions
- The focus is on enabling participants to replicate and expand on what they build during the workshop.

**Intended Outcome**
By the end of the session, attendees will:
- Understand what AI-native development means in practice
- Gain clarity on MCP and how it supports AI system design
- Have hands-on experience building and interacting with a simple AI workflow
- Be equipped to begin experimenting with AI-native approaches in their own projects

**Pre-requisites**
Participants should:
- Have basic familiarity with AI, LLMs, and general prompting concepts. You can start here to get yourself familiar. Link: https://amadeus.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/GHC/pages/3096873543
- Ideally have access to GitHub Copilot. Link: https://amadeus.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/GHC/pages/1436680207 

*This workshop is not just a presentation, it is a practical starting point. We aim to demystify AI-native development and empower engineers to confidently begin integrating AI system components into their workflows.*

Proposal title: The Human Side of AI Prototyping
Description:
We can generate a prototype in seconds. But speed alone does not solve user problems. That requires a truly user centered approach.

In this talk, we will show how Generative AI is transforming design and how our teams use AI prototyping tools to bring ideas to life in minutes, accelerating discovery and experimentation.

However, real impact does not come from speed. It comes from collaboration. When AI is embedded in a cross functional, user centered process where UX, PMs, Developers, and business teams co create, the outcome is not just faster prototypes, but stronger alignment and products that truly deliver value.

Through real world stories and the collaborative recipes we have developed, you will discover how to move beyond the magic of instant prototypes and turn AI into a strategic advantage across the entire product lifecycle.

Proposal title: FinOps - Introduction to FinOps, Product and Service Costs
Description:
Cloud costs keep rising — but where do they come from? How do we translate them into meaningful Product and Service Costs? And how can you make data-driven decisions that actually reduce waste while improving performance?

In this deep-dive session, we demystify the world of FinOps, the operating model adopted by Amadeus to manage, control, and optimize cloud spending at scale. You will learn how raw cloud usage transforms into cost allocation, how Product and Service Cost models are built, and how teams can use FinOps practices to drive accountability, transparency, and efficiency.

This session blends practical examples, live demos, and real scenarios from our own cloud environment (Azure, GCP, AWS).
